transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes (approx)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Romero (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Elysium CISO), Aisha Khan (Elysium Head of Cloud), Robert Li (Elysium Security Architect), Sandra Gomez (Procurement)

Summary (auto): Discussed encryption at rest and in transit, BYOK/HSM provisioning options, key rotation cadence, regional key custody, audit logging for SOC2/ISO purposes, and next steps for a hands-on HSM connector test.

Topics: encryption-at-rest, byok, hsm, kms, key-rotation, data-residency, audit-logs, soc2

Action items (captured): see metadata list

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay everybody hi thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a sec. This is Maya from Redwood, i'm the account exec for Elysium, with me are Luis and Priya on the engineering side.
[00:12] Daniel Park: hey thanks, Daniel here. I'll jump in with the requirements up front — we need to ensure keys for EU workloads are customer‑owned and never leave our control, plus audit trails that map to SOC2 controls.
[00:25] Maya Chen: perfecto. Luis, do you want to outline the BYOK/HSM options briefly?
[00:29] Luis Romero: yeah sure — so there are three common patterns we use: managed KMS with customer key material (BYOK) wrapped by our vault; dedicated HSM in the cloud (HSM as a service) where the key material is provisioned to a tenant-specific HSM instance; and a fully on‑prem HSM with a connector into Redwood Private. Each has tradeoffs.
[00:46] Aisha Khan: when you say "BYOK wrapped by vault" — does that mean the raw key ever leaves our HSM? that's the main question.
[00:52] Luis Romero: good call. For our BYOK flow we support importing key material using a wrap/unwrap protocol — the raw key is generated in your HSM, exported in wrapped form (using a wrapping key), and Redwood only receives the wrapped blob. We rely on KMS import APIs and PKCS11 or an HSM vendor adapter. So the clear answer: raw plaintext key shouldn't be transmitted.
[01:10] Robert Li: are you supporting PKCS#11 and KMIP? our vendor uses both, and sometimes the enterprise HSMs only offer KMIP.
[01:17] Priya Nair: we have tested both PKCS11 and KMIP adapters; there are small differences in the connector behaviour. We'll send the adapter compatibility matrix — but broadly yes, PKCS11 and KMIP are supported, with a short integration shim for some older appliances.
[01:30] Daniel Park: cool. Another thing: we need HSM‑backed keys for signing model artifacts and for encrypting persisted vectors — does Redwood differentiate key usage for signing vs encryption?
[01:41] Luis Romero: yes we recommend separate key types — wrapping keys for encrypting at rest (data keys), and signing keys stored in HSM for digital signatures and key attestations. The runtime can call the HSM for sign/verify operations; the data plane still uses TLS in transit.
[01:52] Sandra Gomez: procurement question — what governance do you have around key escrow and recovery? we have to know if keys can be restored if an admin leaves.
[02:00] Maya Chen: governance: we provide configurable key policies, rotation schedules, and optional escrow— but for BYOK customers, Elysium controls escrow decisions. We'll document options: no-escrow, customer-only escrow, or third-party escrow. We'll include recommended playbooks.
[02:15] Aisha Khan: on rotation cadence — our policy is 90 days for data keys, one year for master signing keys. Does Redwood force rotation or can it honor our existing rotation windows?
[02:24] Luis Romero: you can enforce or opt-out; the platform supports automated rotation with a policy layer. For BYOK, rotation often involves you generating a new key in your HSM and importing the wrapped key material; we can orchestrate the swap to avoid downtime with staged rollouts and prefix/KV cache invalidation. Note: caching/kv cacche was mis-transcribed earlier, but we do have prefix cache invalidation hooks.
[02:45] Robert Li: talk to me about audit logs — we need tamper-evident logs mapped to SOC2 Trust Services Criteria: access to keys, key-usage crypto operations, and admin actions. How are logs exported and retained?
[02:57] Priya Nair: logs are emitted to our audit pipeline; we can stream syslog or push to customer SIEMs via secure forwarders (TLS). Each key operation includes an audit record with operation, key ID, requester principal, and ordinal timestamp. For tamper evidence we support log signing and an append-only store with retention policies configurable for the retention period you need.
[03:18] Daniel Park: also need multi‑factor and RBAC gating on any key rotation or export decisions — our auditors require separation of duties.
[03:25] Luis Romero: Redwood supports RBAC roles and SAML/SSO integration for admin consoles. You can require MFA via your IdP for high-priv actions; we also support step-up auth for HSM provisioning workflows.
[03:38] Aisha Khan: data residency — can keys for EU workloads be physically provisioned only in eu‑west and never copied to us‑east?
[03:45] Maya Chen: yes, region‑pinned key material is supported. For hosted customers we can ensure HSM instances are only in a set of regions; if you use Private, you can run the HSM in your VPC in the EU. We'll need the specific list of regions.
[03:58] Robert Li: regarding transport encryption in transit — we require TLS1.3 and mutual TLS for high‑priv operations. Does Redwood require mTLS between the private connector and your control plane?
[04:06] Priya Nair: we support mTLS for connector channels and the control plane; all connections for key operations use mTLS and are logged. Internal services use zero‑trust links and TLS.
[04:15] Daniel Park: vendor attestations — do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 certs? our procurement needs to see the latest reports.
[04:22] Maya Chen: Redwood has SOC2 Type II and is audited for ISO27001 scope across core services. We'll share redacted reports and the compliance package. Note: for Private deployments we can provide additional evidence as part of the enterprise contract.
[04:34] Sandra Gomez: what about cross‑border key export controls? if a key originates in the EU, can Redwood do a backup to a US region for DR?
[04:42] Luis Romero: by default we won't move region‑pinned key material. For DR you can either adopt a policy to replicate wrapped backups to a secondary region under your control, or run in dedicated HSMs in multiple regions. We'll document options with the legal team's input.
[04:58] Aisha Khan: integration testing — we want a lab where we can validate the import flow and do a dummy sign request. How long is the setup?
[05:05] Luis Romero: the hands‑on lab is typically 30–60 minutes if you have an HSM test appliance or a vendor cloud HSM project. We'll provide sample scripts for PKCS11 and KMIP. We'll also share a test vector sheet.
[05:17] Robert Li: are you able to provide a HSM signing attestation chain (certificate of key origin)? our auditors want evidence the key was created in an HSM.
[05:25] Priya Nair: yes, HSMs issue attestation objects; we can store and surface the attestations in the console and include them in audit exports. For some vendors it's vendor-signed attestation; for customer on‑prem HSMs you can provide the attestation blob.
[05:37] Daniel Park: one subtlety — we have a third‑party escrow requirement for certain keys. Can Redwood interop with an escrow provider without exposing plaintext to Redwood?
[05:44] Luis Romero: yes — we can support an external escrow by accepting wrapped key blobs and storing them encrypted under your escrow provider's public key. We never unwrap plaintext unless explicitly requested under your policy.
[05:55] Maya Chen: quick note on model privacy: when you call the inference API, we keep payloads encrypted in transit (TLS) and at rest; vector DBs can have envelope encryption where the data key is wrapped by your HSM key. That keeps the model input and embeddings protected under your key.
[06:14] Sandra Gomez: procurement again — what's the SLA on key‑operation latency? some of our RL inferencing pipelines need sub‑50ms sign/verify.
[06:22] Luis Romero: for HSM-backed sign operations, latency depends on HSM vendor and network; dedicated HSM in region can meet sub 50ms in many cases. We'll run benchmarks during the lab against your expected QPS. For high throughput we recommend local HSM pool with batching and async sign where possible.
[06:39] Robert Li: any gotchas with Kubernetes/gpu runtimes and the key connector? our infra team uses k8s sidecars and we want minimal changes.
[06:46] Priya Nair: the connector can run as a sidecar or an external service in the pod network; we have examples for k8s, and support socket-based PKCS11 mounting if you need. We'll send the k8s manifest example.
[07:02] Maya Chen: ok i want to recap next steps — we'll send the BYOK runbook, HSM checklist, SOC2/ISO artifacts, and schedule the hands‑on lab. Anything else?
[07:12] Daniel Park: please include the sample audit log schema and retention options. Also include examples of RBAC roles and step-up auth flows.
[07:20] Maya Chen: will do. Luis, any technical caveats we should call out?
[07:24] Luis Romero: just that older appliances sometimes need an adapter, and rotation workflows require coordination to avoid cache stomps; we'll cover safe rollouts in the runbook. Also note latency is vendor and region dependent.
[07:36] Aisha Khan: ok thanks everyone — we'll review the runbook and come back with region list.
[07:41] Maya Chen: great thanks, we'll follow up with links.
[07:44] Sandra Gomez: thanks all.

End of transcript.
